ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: BF threshold categories collapsed — must know standard BF interpretation scales
ground_truth.original_snippet: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.1: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.1 - 0.33: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis. 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 3 – 10: substantial evidence for the...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 3 – 10: substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis, >10: strong evidence for the a...
ground_truth.description: Collapsed BF null thresholds — BF between 0.1-0.33 (substantial) now classified as 'strong' evidence for null; systematically inflates null conclusions throughout paper

matched_finding.subcategory: Bayes-factor evidence labels are asymmetric around 1
matched_finding.description: Bayes-factor evidence labels are asymmetric around 1: If Bayes factors above 1 favour inclusion or the alternative, the null-side labels should be reciprocal. A BF of 0.5 is the inverse of BF = 2, so it is only anecdotal evidence in the opposite direction, not substantial evidence. Likewise, BF < 0.33 corresponds to just over 3:1 evidence for the null, not the reciprocal of the usual >10 “strong” threshold. Revise the interpretation scale to use reciprocal ranges, for example 0.33–1 as anecdotal evidence for the null, 0.1–0.33 as substantial, and <0.1 as strong.
matched_finding.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type. Within this analysis, the posterior odds of all different combinations the three factors and their interactions are compared to the prior explanatory value of each model. Based on this analysis, we selected the model with the best fit, reporting the BFm. Individual model components (main effects and interactions) were additionally evaluated based on their BFincl across all models. Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF $<0.33$ : strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33-1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1-3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, $3-10$ : substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis, $>10$ : strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Interference display proportion matching absent — must understand balanced interference logic
ground_truth.original_snippet: Furthermore, it contained the same proportion of real and pseudo-letters as the memory display.
ground_truth.description: Removed requirement that interference display matches proportion of real/pseudo letters — unbalanced display could differentially strengthen real-letter representations, confounding expectation-based illusion account

matched_finding.subcategory: Balance of the intervening displays is left unclear in Experiment 3
matched_finding.description: Balance of the intervening displays is left unclear in Experiment 3: Experiment 3 is presented as the balanced-stimulus test, but this sentence only states that the memory displays were balanced. If the irrelevant intervening screens retained the Experiment 2 composition of 4 real and 2 pseudo-letters, then participants still received unequal exposure during the interference display. If those screens were also balanced, say so explicitly. Either way, the composition of the intervening displays should be reported because it is part of the exposure and interference manipulation.
matched_finding.quote: The memory displays and irrelevant intervening screens were the same as in Experiment 2 except that the memory displays always consisted of 3 real and 3 pseudo-letters.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Binary confidence scale collapses moderate with high — must know confidence resolution matters for illusion claims
ground_truth.original_snippet: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).
ground_truth.description: Changed 4-point to 2-point confidence scale — 'high confidence' now conflates moderate and high certainty; inflates high-confidence illusion rates with uncertain responses

matched_finding.description: Contradictory confidence scales: The Figure 1 caption and the Experiment 1 Procedure section give contradictory confidence scales: the caption gives a 4-point scale (\$1=$ guess, \$4=$ certainty), whereas the Procedure section gives a 2-point scale (\$1=$ guess, \$2=$ certain). Since the Experiment 1 analyses are restricted to high-confidence trials, the paper should clarify the actual scale and the criterion used to classify a response as high confidence.
matched_finding.quote: In all conditions, after offset of the second letter display, the participant first indicated the identity of the letter at the cued location in the memory display. Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment ( $1=$ guess, $4=$ certainty).

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Temporal inference sentence removed — but premise remains; must notice the logical chain is broken
ground_truth.original_snippet: Therefore, if the number of reported illusions increases as the retention interval increases, this is best explained by memory-related processes taking place during the retention interval, so during STM storage itself, and not in the perceptual or encoding process.
ground_truth.description: Deleted the critical inferential sentence linking delay-dependent increase to memory (not perception) processes — severs the causal logic that makes the multi-delay design interpretable

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: BF=6 stopping rule vs BF>10 'strong evidence' threshold — must cross-reference
ground_truth.original_snippet: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.
ground_truth.description: Changed BF stopping threshold from 10 to 6 — inconsistent with paper's own 'strong evidence' threshold (>10); study would have stopped at merely 'substantial' evidence

matched_finding.subcategory: The optional stopping contrast is not reproducible
matched_finding.description: The optional stopping contrast is not reproducible: This rule fixed the sample size, so the exact test must be recoverable. “The comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets” could mean a paired test on two illusion rates, a difference-of-differences, or a follow-up to the interaction. The direction of the Bayes factor, prior, and software settings are also missing. Add the exact participant-level contrast, state whether the threshold was BF10 or BF01, and report the prior specification used for the sequential test.
matched_finding.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t -test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

ground_truth.original_snippet: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. If the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the patte...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent w...
ground_truth.description: Replaced entire empirical response bias analysis (confidence-by-error-type dissociation with percentages) with vague dismissal — removes the load-bearing alternative-explanation test

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Creates internal contradiction detectable within the paper
ground_truth.description: Changed stimulus size from 1.16° to 0.05° — below visual acuity threshold, contradicts successful task performance reported in results

matched_finding.subcategory: Impossible stimulus dimensions in training task
matched_finding.description: Impossible stimulus dimensions in training task: The reported training-stimulus dimensions, $0.05^{\circ} \times 0.01^{\circ}$, appear implausibly small for peripheral orientation discrimination at a radius of $4.68^{\circ}$. If taken literally, these rectangles would be only about 3 by 0.6 arcminutes, making it difficult to reconcile the method with the requirement that participants exceed 75% accuracy in training. This is likely a typographical error in the reported stimulus size and should be corrected for reproducibility.
matched_finding.quote: The memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles ( $0.05^{\circ} \times 0.01^{\circ}$ in size) which had horizontal, vertical or oblique ( $45^{\circ}$ or $135^{\circ}$ ) orientations.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: FTT 'inhibit'→'facilitate' reverses prediction — must know FTT's actual prediction about similarity
ground_truth.original_snippet: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories
ground_truth.modified_snippet: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories
ground_truth.description: Reversed FTT prediction from 'inhibit' to 'facilitate' — paper no longer differentiates its account from FTT; removes key theoretical contribution

matched_finding.subcategory: FTT similarity argument reverses its own prediction
matched_finding.description: FTT similarity argument reverses its own prediction: The Fuzzy Trace Theory comparison contains a reversed entailment. If FTT is said to predict that high target–counterpart similarity should facilitate false memories, then the combination of extremely similar stimuli and abundant false memories is consistent with that stated prediction, not inconsistent with it. The intended tension may instead concern the asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors.
matched_finding.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant. Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Training exclusion dropped from Exps 2-4 without stated justification — must notice cross-experiment procedural change
ground_truth.original_snippet: Since only 10% of participants were excluded from participating in the main experiment based on the training scores, the training procedure was not part of Experiments 2, 3 and 4 in order to not make the overall time on task too long.
ground_truth.description: Removed justification for dropping training/screening from Exps 2-4 — undisclosed procedural change; those experiments lack minimum-competence screening that Exp 1 had

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: 23+5=28 doesn't equal stated N=40 — arithmetic contradiction
ground_truth.original_snippet: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)
ground_truth.modified_snippet: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)
ground_truth.description: Changed exclusions from 17 to 5 — hides 42.5% attrition rate (17/40); true rate raises concerns about selective retention of overconfident responders; 23+5=28 doesn't equal 40

matched_finding.description: Unaccounted participant attrition: The Experiment 1 participant accounting is inconsistent. The Participants section says 40 participants remained after training, but the Analysis section reports an inclusion of 23 participants and says 5 participants were excluded for too few high-confidence critical trials. That accounts for only 28 of the 40 participants, leaving 12 participants unexplained. The paper should clarify the full participant flow and the final sample size used in the Experiment 1 analyses.
matched_finding.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants ( 28 female; age range 19-30 years, average age 22.2 years) all had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
